title: Achan's Sin and the Defeat at Ai
summary: Achan of the tribe of Judah secretly takes some of the devoted things from Jericho, and the LORD's anger burns against Israel. Confident after Jericho, Joshua sends a small force against Ai, and it is routed, with about thirty-six Israelites killed. Joshua and the elders mourn before the ark, and the LORD reveals that Israel has broken the covenant. Through a process of selection, tribe by tribe, Achan is identified; he confesses to taking a cloak, silver, and gold, and he and his household are stoned and burned in the Valley of Achor.
story: Jericho ended with Joshua's fame spreading through the land. Chapter 7 opens with a single word of contrast, however, and tells the reader what Joshua does not yet know: someone has taken what was devoted to the LORD. The chapter reverses the story's momentum. Israel, which watched Jericho's walls fall, now flees from a small town, and it is Israel's heart that melts like water (verse 5), the same image used of the Canaanites in 2:11 and 5:1. The lesson is that the LORD's presence cannot be presumed on. Israel's enemies are not the only ones under judgment. Once the sin is dealt with, chapter 8 will show Israel taking Ai under God's direction.
historical:
Ai lay in the central hill country near Bethel, to the east of it (verse 2), on the route climbing from Jericho into the heart of the land. Its name means the ruin, and it is usually identified with et-Tell, a large mound northeast of Jerusalem. Excavations at et-Tell (by Judith Marquet-Krause in the 1930s and Joseph Callaway in the 1960s) found a major Early Bronze Age city destroyed long before Joshua, and no occupation in the Late Bronze Age. Scholars respond in different ways. Some conclude that the story explains an old ruin rather than recording a battle. Others argue that Ai was located elsewhere; excavators at Khirbet el-Maqatir, nearby, have proposed that site as the Ai of Joshua. Others suggest that the Canaanites of Bethel used the old ruin as a defensive outpost. The question is unresolved.

Beth-aven (verse 2) means house of wickedness, and Hosea later uses it as a mocking name for Bethel (Hosea 4:15). Shinar (verse 21) is the biblical name for Babylonia (Genesis 11:2), so Achan's cloak was an imported luxury garment. Two hundred shekels of silver and a fifty-shekel bar of gold were substantial wealth; a shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven or twelve grams, since coins did not yet exist.
cultural:
In the ancient world a family or community was bound together in ways modern individualists find difficult to grasp. What a member did could implicate the whole. Israel's covenant language reflects this: when one man steals from the ban, God says Israel has sinned (verse 11). Joshua's response follows the customs of mourning: tearing clothes, falling face down, and putting dust on the head (verse 6).

The process of identifying the guilty man by tribe, clan, family, and individual (verses 14-18) reflects how Israel's society was organized in nested kinship groups. The text does not say how the LORD selected, but it was probably by lot, perhaps using the Urim and Thummim (compare 1 Samuel 14:38-42). Joshua's words to Achan, give glory to the LORD and make confession (verse 19), were a formula for urging a person to tell the truth under oath, acknowledging God as the witness. Stoning was a communal punishment in which all Israel took part, so the community itself removed the guilt from its midst. The large pile of rocks raised over Achan (verse 26), like the memorial stones at the Jordan, served as a lasting reminder. Deuteronomy 13:12-18 had commanded that anyone who turned a city to idolatry should be burned with all its goods as devoted to the LORD, and Achan's punishment treats him as having brought the ban on himself.
literary: The chapter opens with the narrator telling the reader what the characters do not know (verse 1), which creates painful irony throughout the failed attack and Joshua's lament. Joshua's prayer (verses 7-9) echoes the grumbling of the wilderness generation, wishing they had stayed on the other side of the Jordan, and ends with concern for God's great name. God's answer is abrupt: “Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face?” The selection process is told slowly and deliberately, narrowing step by step to one man, which heightens the tension. Achan's confession follows a telling sequence: “I saw ... I coveted them and took them” (verse 21), the same pattern as Eve in Genesis 3:6. The chapter plays on Achan's name and the Hebrew verb akar, to trouble: Joshua asks why he has troubled Israel, and the place is named the Valley of Achor, valley of trouble (verses 25-26). First Chronicles 2:7 even calls him Achar, the troubler of Israel.

outline.t: Achan takes devoted things and the LORD is angry
The LORD reveals the sin and commands consecration
Judgment in the Valley of Achor

doctrines.note: Achan's sin moves from seeing to coveting to taking to hiding, and the effect reaches far beyond him. The chapter shows sin as both personal and communal: one man's disobedience brings defeat on the whole people.
God will not be with Israel while devoted things remain among them (verse 12). His presence among his people requires that they deal honestly with sin rather than hide it.
Joshua urges Achan to give glory to God by confessing. Confession acknowledges the truth before God. Here it does not avert judgment, but it does honor God and clear the way for Israel's restoration.
The judgment that fell on Jericho falls on an Israelite who takes what was devoted. God's justice is not partial toward his own people.

words.note: Maal, to act unfaithfully or treacherously. It describes a breach of trust, especially against God regarding holy things. It is the chapter's first verdict: Israel acted unfaithfully regarding the devoted things (verse 1). Chronicles uses the same word for the unfaithfulness that led to exile.
Chamad, to desire or covet. It is the verb of the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17). Achan's I coveted them (verse 21) names the inner root of the outward theft.

Akar, to trouble or bring disaster. Joshua warned in 6:18 that taking devoted things would bring trouble on the camp, and here Achan has done so (verse 25). The word gives the Valley of Achor its name.

Cherem, the devoted thing or ban. It appears again and again in the chapter. The irony is sharp: by taking what was devoted to destruction, Achan made himself and Israel devoted to destruction (verse 12).

christ: The Valley of Achor did not remain only a place of judgment in Israel's memory. Hosea 2:15 promises that God will “make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope,” and Isaiah 65:10 pictures it as a resting place for herds. The prophets saw that God could turn the place of trouble into a door of restoration. The New Testament develops this hope in Christ, who took the curse and judgment of sin on himself so that sinners could be forgiven rather than destroyed (Galatians 3:13, 2 Corinthians 5:21). Some readers also notice a parallel in Acts 5, where Ananias and Sapphira secretly keep back part of what they claimed to give to God and die, a sobering sign at the church's beginning, like Achan's at Israel's, that God's holiness among his people is not to be trifled with. These are thematic connections drawn from the wider canon, not predictions in Joshua 7.

hard.q: Why were Achan's children and possessions destroyed with him, when Deuteronomy 24:16 says children should not die for their fathers' sins?
hard.a: Deuteronomy 24:16 does forbid ordinary courts from punishing children for their parents' crimes, so the question is real. Interpreters answer in a few ways. Some argue that Achan's family must have known of the theft, since the goods were buried under the family tent, and so shared in the guilt. Others emphasize that this case falls under the special law of the ban rather than ordinary justice: what is devoted to destruction, including a person who has taken devoted things, is wholly given over, as Deuteronomy 13:15-17 required for an apostate town. Others point to the ancient understanding of the household as a single unit, in which the head's action implicated all. Some note that the Hebrew of verse 25 is not fully clear about who was stoned and burned, though the plain sense includes the family. Readers who find none of these answers fully satisfying often observe that the text itself presents the event as extraordinary and terrible, and that later Scripture (Ezekiel 18) insists that each person is judged for their own sin.

questions: Achan's sin began with seeing and coveting before it became stealing. Where do you notice that same progression in your own temptations?
Israel's defeat came because of one man's hidden sin. How do private choices affect the communities we belong to?
Hosea later speaks of the Valley of Achor becoming a door of hope. How has God brought something good out of a place of failure in your life?
